Yes. I reviewed the current Printful documentation. The URL you provided is specifically useful if you want to build your **own product-design/mockup interface** rather than simply display pre-generated Printful product images.

The key architectural point is that Printful separates **product/variant selection**, **print-area/template discovery**, **design positioning**, and **mockup generation**. The mockup operation itself is asynchronous. ([developers.printful.com](https://developers.printful.com/docs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

## What the Printful API gives us

For the workflow in your link, the important API chain is essentially:

**Product → Variant → Technique → Printfile → Layout Template → Design Position → Mockup Task → Generated Mockup**

For example, Printful's layout-template endpoint is:

`GET /mockup-generator/templates/{product_id}`

and it accepts a `technique` parameter when the product supports multiple production techniques. Without specifying one, Printful says DTG is used as the default for layouts having multiple techniques. ([developers.printful.com](https://developers.printful.com/docs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

A returned template contains values such as `template_width`, `template_height`, `print_area_width`, `print_area_height`, `print_area_top`, `print_area_left`, and `printfile_id`. Those values are exactly what a browser-based designer needs to draw the printable area and translate the customer's visual positioning into Printful coordinates. ([developers.printful.com](https://developers.printful.com/docs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Printful also provides `variant_mapping`, which connects a selected catalog variant with the correct template/placement. This matters because we should **not hard-code one print area for every shirt/color/variant**. ([developers.printful.com](https://developers.printful.com/docs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The mockup is then requested through:

`POST /mockup-generator/create-task/{product_id}`

with the selected `variant_ids`, artwork URL, placement and optional position coordinates. Printful returns a `task_key`; your application then checks:

`GET /mockup-generator/task?task_key=...`

for completion. Printful specifically advises that the first result check should not occur sooner than about 10 seconds. ([developers.printful.com](https://developers.printful.com/docs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Another important production issue: generated mockup URLs are temporary, so your application should persist the finished assets to your own storage rather than treating Printful's returned URL as permanent. ([developers.printful.com](https://developers.printful.com/docs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Printful also has a newer **Mockup Generator v2** architecture. It formalizes catalog products, variants, design data, mockup styles, asynchronous tasks, and webhook completion notifications. ([developers.printful.com](https://developers.printful.com/docs/v2-preview/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

[Printful API Documentation](https://developers.printful.com/docs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Given your existing Next.js work, I would not have VS Code build merely a "Printful API example." I would build a reusable **Printful Product Designer module** with a server-side Printful API layer.

The browser never receives the Printful access token.

```text
                           │

```

## Prompt:
can you explain in simple terms what this new api version and the prompt provided for my storefront. It sound more than syncing products on printful.

## Response:
gpt-5-6

Yes. You are reading it correctly. **The prompt I provided goes considerably beyond simply syncing Printful products into your storefront.**

Think of the difference this way:

### Basic Printful integration — “Sell Printful products”

Your storefront connects to Printful and essentially says:

```text
PRINTFUL
   │
   │ Product information
   │ Variants
   │ Colors
   │ Sizes
   │ Images
   │ Prices
   ▼
YOUR STOREFRONT

Customer selects:
Black → XL → Buy
        │
        ▼
      Stripe
        │
        ▼
Order sent to Printful
        │
        ▼
Printful manufactures + ships
```

That is the traditional POD storefront model.

You create the shirt/design in Printful beforehand. Your site **syncs the finished product** and sells it.

For your storefront, that may already accomplish most of what you need.

---

## What the Mockup Generator API adds

The API documentation you gave me is about something more sophisticated.

Instead of Printful being the only place where products are designed, **your website can participate in creating the product design**.

For example, imagine a CountyBuys customer selects:

> Illinois → Will County → Black Shirt → XL

Your storefront could potentially generate the appropriate design/mockup dynamically rather than requiring you to manually create every possible combination beforehand.

The architecture becomes:

```text
                    PRINTFUL
                       │
                blank products
                       │
                       ▼
CUSTOMER ─────► YOUR STOREFRONT
                    │
                    │
             Select product
             Select color
             Select size
             Add/select design
             Position artwork
                    │
                    ▼
             PRINTFUL MOCKUP API
                    │
             "Show me what this
              would look like."
                    │
                    ▼
              Generated image
                    │
                    ▼
               CUSTOMER
```

That is why the prompt contained things such as **print areas, coordinates, templates, techniques, placements, artwork positioning and mockup generation**.

Those aren't required for ordinary product synchronization.

---

# The important difference for your storefront

There are really **three levels** you could build.

| Level | What your storefront does | Complexity |
|---|---|---:|
| **1 — Product Sync** | Import existing Printful products and sell them | Low |
| **2 — Dynamic Mockups** | Your storefront asks Printful to generate product images dynamically | Medium |
| **3 — Product Designer** | Customer creates/customizes the product directly on your site | High |

The prompt I gave you was essentially **Level 3**.

Your original request based on the Mockup Generator documentation led me in that direction because the layout-template API is particularly useful for building a designer.

But you may **not need Level 3 yet**.

### Level 1: Product synchronization

Suppose you create this in Printful:

```text
PRODUCT
County Pride T-Shirt

Design:
"HOME IS WHERE THE COUNTY IS"

Variants:
S
M
L
XL
2XL

Colors:
Black
White
Navy
Gray
```

Your storefront imports it.

Customer sees:

```text
County Pride T-Shirt
$24.99

Color: [Black ▼]
Size:  [XL ▼]

[ADD TO CART]
```

Customer pays.

Your backend sends the Printful variant/order information to Printful.

Printful prints and ships it.

**No mockup-generator API is required for that basic workflow.**

---

# Level 2 is where this gets interesting

This may eventually be particularly useful for a storefront with lots of localized products.

Imagine you have:

```text
3,000 counties
×
10 shirt designs
×
5 colors
```

You probably don't want to manually create:

**150,000 Printful products.**

Instead your database could contain:

```text
DESIGN
"Born & Raised"

LOCATION
Will County

PRODUCT
Bella Canvas Shirt

COLOR
Black
```

Then your system asks Printful:

```text
Generate a mockup of:

Bella Canvas 3001
Black
Front printing

Artwork:
Will County
Born & Raised
```

Printful returns the mockup.

Your customer sees:

```text
┌───────────────────────┐
│                       │
│       T-SHIRT         │
│                       │
│     WILL COUNTY       │
│     BORN & RAISED     │
│                       │
└───────────────────────┘
```

Now you are using Printful more like a **manufacturing engine** behind your storefront rather than simply treating Printful as your product catalog.

That can dramatically reduce how many finished products you need to maintain.

---

# Level 3 — what my original prompt built

The original prompt goes another step.

It gives the customer something approaching:

```text
       PRODUCT DESIGNER

       ┌───────────────┐
       │               │
       │   T-SHIRT     │
       │               │
       │  ┌─────────┐  │
       │  │ Artwork │  │
       │  │         │  │
       │  └─────────┘  │
       │               │
       └───────────────┘

Upload Image

Placement:
[Front ▼]

Technique:
[DTG ▼]

Size:
[──────●──]

Position:
[ drag artwork ]

        [GENERATE MOCKUP]
```

That is essentially building **your own mini Printful product designer inside your storefront**.

The Printful layout-template API tells your application:

> "On this particular shirt, this rectangle is where printing is allowed."

Your JavaScript then keeps the customer's design inside that area.

That's why the API exposes dimensions such as:

```text
template_width
template_height

print_area_width
print_area_height

print_area_top
print_area_left
```

Those numbers allow your storefront to understand:

```text
          SHIRT

    ┌─────────────────┐
    │                 │
    │    ┌───────┐    │
    │    │ PRINT │    │
    │    │ AREA  │    │
    │    └───────┘    │
    │                 │
    └─────────────────┘
```

That functionality is unnecessary if **you create all designs yourself**.

---

# And what is "v2"?

The newer Mockup Generator API is essentially Printful evolving this capability into a more structured system.

The conceptual workflow becomes:

```text
Catalog Product
      ↓
Variant
      ↓
Placement
      ↓
Design Data
      ↓
Mockup Style
      ↓
Generate Task
      ↓
Printful processes it
      ↓
Completed Mockup
```

A significant concept here is **asynchronous generation**.

Your server doesn't say:

> Give me the image.

and immediately receive it.

It says:

> Please create this mockup.

Printful responds approximately:

```text
task_id: ABC123
status: pending
```

Your system later asks:

```text
Is ABC123 finished?
```

Printful eventually responds:

```text
status: completed

mockups:
   front.jpg
   back.jpg
```

That architecture makes more sense when a storefront is generating products dynamically.

---

# What I would do for your storefront

I would actually **reduce the scope of the first prompt**.

Start here:

```text
PHASE 1
PRINTFUL PRODUCT SYNC

Printful
   ↓
Products
   ↓
Variants
   ↓
Images
   ↓
Your Database
   ↓
Your Storefront
   ↓
Cart
   ↓
Stripe
   ↓
Printful Order
```

But design the backend so we can later add:

```text
PHASE 2
DYNAMIC MOCKUPS

           ↓

PHASE 3
CUSTOMIZATION

           ↓

PHASE 4
FULL PRODUCT DESIGNER
```

That avoids spending development time building a Canva-like designer before the storefront needs one.

And there is an especially valuable middle ground for a storefront with **personalized/localized merchandise**: **Phase 2 does not have to expose a designer to the customer.** Your backend could automatically compose the appropriate county/name/design and ask Printful to generate the mockup. The customer simply sees the finished product. That gives you much of the scalability benefit without the complexity of a customer-facing design editor.

So yes: **if your immediate objective is “connect my storefront to Printful and sync products,” the previous VS Code prompt is overbuilt for Phase 1.** I would replace it with a narrower Printful Product Sync + Order Fulfillment prompt, while deliberately preparing the architecture for the Mockup Generator later.

## Prompt:

## Response:
gpt-5-6

Yes. A **product catalog is the important distinction**. You can have a large Printful catalog available in your storefront **without syncing thousands of finished products into Printful first**.

There are actually two different catalogs to think about.

### 1. Printful's catalog - blank products

Printful has a catalog of products it can manufacture:

```text
PRINTFUL CATALOG

T-Shirts
 ├─ Bella + Canvas 3001
 ├─ Gildan 5000
 └─ Comfort Colors 1717

Hoodies
 ├─ Gildan 18500
 └─ ...

Hats
Mugs
Posters
Phone Cases
Bags
etc.
```

Through the Catalog API, your storefront can retrieve information about those products: product IDs, variants, sizes, colors, images, availability, and related production information.

This is **not the same as syncing your designed products**.

### 2. Your storefront catalog - products you actually sell

Your customer should probably not browse Printful's entire manufacturing catalog directly. Instead, your application can maintain its own curated catalog:

```text
YOUR STOREFRONT CATALOG

Men
 ├─ T-Shirts
 ├─ Hoodies
 └─ Sweatshirts

Women
 ├─ T-Shirts
 ├─ Hoodies
 └─ Tanks

Home
 ├─ Mugs
 ├─ Posters
 └─ Pillows

Accessories
 ├─ Hats
 ├─ Bags
 └─ Phone Cases
```

Each storefront product can reference the underlying Printful catalog product.

For example:

```text
YOUR DATABASE

Store Product
────────────────────────
Name: Premium County Tee
Category: T-Shirts
Price: $27.99

Printful Product ID: 71
        │
        ▼
PRINTFUL
Bella + Canvas 3001

Variants:
Black / S
Black / M
Black / L
Navy / S
Navy / M
...
```

That is the architecture I would recommend.

## You don't necessarily want "sync everything"

There are three concepts that are easy to confuse:

```text
PRINTFUL CATALOG
Blank merchandise Printful manufactures
        │
        ▼
YOUR CATALOG
Products you've chosen to offer
        │
        ▼
YOUR DESIGNS
Artwork applied to those products
        │
        ▼
PRINTFUL FULFILLMENT
What gets manufactured after purchase
```

Those should remain separate.

For example, suppose Printful offers 400+ product types. Your storefront doesn't need to create 400 Printful store products.

You could select only:

```text
Bella + Canvas 3001
Gildan 5000
Gildan 18500
Premium Hoodie
Coffee Mug
Poster
Hat
Tote Bag
```

Your database stores those as your approved **base products**.

Then your designs can sit on top of them.

---

## This is where the newer API becomes useful

Suppose you have this artwork:

```text
WILL COUNTY
EST. 1836
```

You don't necessarily need this structure:

```text
Printful Product #1
Will County Black Shirt

Printful Product #2
Will County White Shirt

Printful Product #3
Will County Hoodie

Printful Product #4
Will County Sweatshirt
```

Instead your storefront could understand:

```text
DESIGN
Will County / Est. 1836
       │
       ├──────────────┐
       ▼              ▼
Bella 3001         Gildan Hoodie
       │              │
       ▼              ▼
Mockup API        Mockup API
       │              │
       ▼              ▼
Product page      Product page
```

This allows **your database to become the real product catalog**, while Printful becomes the manufacturing provider.

That is much more scalable.

## What the customer would see

Nothing needs to look complicated.

They might simply browse:

```text
SHOP

┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐
│   IMAGE   │  │   IMAGE   │  │   IMAGE   │
│           │  │           │  │           │
│ County    │  │ County    │  │ County    │
│ T-Shirt   │  │ Hoodie    │  │ Mug       │
│           │  │           │  │           │
│ $24.99    │  │ $44.99    │  │ $17.99    │
└───────────┘  └───────────┘  └───────────┘
```

They don't need to know that behind the scenes you have:

```text
Storefront Product
       ↓
Your Database
       ↓
Printful Catalog Product
       ↓
Printful Variant
       ↓
Your Artwork
       ↓
Printful Mockup
       ↓
Printful Fulfillment
```

That's an implementation detail.

## I would therefore change our phases slightly

Rather than making Phase 1 merely "sync Printful products," I'd make it:

**Phase 1 - Printful Catalog Integration**

Printful's catalog feeds your administrative system:

```text
Printful Catalog API
        ↓
Import/catalog browser
        ↓
Choose products to sell
        ↓
Your Product Catalog
        ↓
Categories / Collections
        ↓
Pricing
        ↓
Storefront
```

Then:

**Phase 2 - Designs + Mockups**

```text
Your Designs
      +
Catalog Product
      ↓
Printful Mockup Generator
      ↓
Store Product
```

Then:

**Phase 3 - Fulfillment**

```text
Customer Purchase
      ↓
Stripe
      ↓
Your Order
      ↓
Printful Order API
      ↓
Manufacturing
      ↓
Shipping
      ↓
Tracking
```

And only if you want it later:

**Phase 4 - Customer Designer**

```text
Upload artwork
Customize text
Move design
Resize design
Choose placement
Generate preview
```

### The key architectural decision

I would make **your storefront database the source of truth for what you sell**, not Printful.

Printful should be the source of truth for **what Printful can manufacture**.

That distinction gives you considerably more control. It also means that later, your architecture could support another POD provider without rebuilding your storefront:

```text
                 YOUR CATALOG
                      │
            ┌─────────┴─────────┐
            │                   │
        Printful             Printify
            │                   │
        Supplier A           Supplier B
```

Your customer still sees one unified catalog.

For your immediate build, I therefore recommend **Catalog API + curated storefront catalog first**, not the full Product Designer prompt I gave earlier. The Mockup Generator then becomes a second layer that enhances your catalog rather than being the foundation of it.

## Overall status

### The main problem: variants

This is the most important discovery.

Currently:

```text
STORE PRODUCT
UUID owned by your storefront
        │
        └── variants JSONB
                 │
                 └── id = PRINTFUL VARIANT ID
```

The Printful ID becomes the variant ID placed into the customer's cart, and checkout later sends that same ID directly back to Printful. There is no storefront-owned variant identity. `AUDIT-REPORT.md`

That conflicts with the architecture we just documented.

We want:

```text
STORE PRODUCT
UUID
   │
   ▼
STORE VARIANT
UUID
   │
   ├── color
   ├── size
   ├── price
   │
   └── printful_variant_id
              │
              ▼
           PRINTFUL
```

Then the cart contains **your variant UUID**, not Printful's.

At fulfillment:

```text
Customer buys
      ↓
Store Variant UUID
      ↓
Database lookup
      ↓
printful_variant_id
      ↓
Printful fulfillment
```

That single change establishes a genuine boundary between your storefront and Printful.

The audit correctly identifies this as the highest-priority architectural change. `AUDIT-REPORT.md`

## Your existing catalog is better than we expected

You already have:

```text
products
categories
```

```text
content_locked
is_personalizable
```

So we're **not creating a product catalog from zero**. `AUDIT-REPORT.md`

The issue is that products currently enter the database almost exclusively by syncing Printful store products:

```text
Printful Store
     ↓
Sync
     ↓
products table
     ↓
Storefront
```

We eventually want:

```text
                 YOUR CATALOG
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        │             │             │
     Product       Variants      Designs
        │             │             │
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      │
                 Provider Data
                      │
                   Printful
```

The existing `products` table can remain at the center of that architecture.

## Another important finding: Printify is effectively gone

This is good news.

There is **zero runtime Printify code remaining in `src/`**. The old Printify material consists mainly of stale configuration, documentation, installation SQL, reset SQL, environment examples, and scripts. `AUDIT-REPORT.md`

You now have two Printful integrations, but they aren't actually duplicates.


The first uses Printful's **store products**. The second uses the broader **Printful catalog** and Mockup Generator capabilities. The audit found no meaningful functional overlap requiring consolidation. `AUDIT-REPORT.md`

Right now, artwork uploaded through the new designer goes into Supabase Storage, but there is **no database record representing that design**.

# What Phase 2 should actually do

Based on this audit, I would narrow Phase 2 rather than trying to build everything simultaneously.

### Phase 2A - Stabilize the architecture

```text
SECURITY
    ↓
Protect Printful mutation APIs

CLEANUP
    ↓
Remove stale Printify config references

VARIANT NORMALIZATION
    ↓
Create product_variants
    ↓
Stable storefront UUID
    ↓
Map to printful_variant_id

CART
    ↓
Use storefront variant UUID

FULFILLMENT
    ↓
Resolve storefront UUID
    ↓
Printful variant ID
    ↓
Submit to Printful
```

That gives us the foundation.

### Phase 2B - Make the catalog truly storefront-owned

Then:

```text
products
    │
    ├── slug
    ├── meta_title
    ├── meta_description
    │
    ├── product_variants
    │
    └── product images
```

And provide an independent product creation path rather than requiring Printful synchronization for every product.

### Phase 2C - Design library

Then:

```text
designs
   │
   ├── artwork
   ├── metadata
   └── reusable assets
          │
          ▼
    product_designs
          │
     ┌────┴────┐
     ▼         ▼
   Shirt     Hoodie
```

### Phase 2D - Catalog builder

And this is where everything we've built comes together:

```text
ADMIN
  │
  ▼
Browse Printful Catalog
  │
  ▼
Select Blank Product
  │
  ▼
Choose Variants
  │
  ▼
Choose Design
  │
  ▼
Generate Mockups
  │
  ▼
Set Retail Price
  │
  ▼
Category / SEO
  │
  ▼
Publish
  │
  ▼
YOUR STOREFRONT
```

That's the system I think you were originally envisioning when you asked me about having a **product catalog**.

## One adjustment to the audit's recommendation

The audit recommends immediately putting `<ProductDesigner />` at `/admin/designer`. `AUDIT-REPORT.md`

I would **not make that the priority yet**.

The designer works. We know it's there.

What it currently lacks is a meaningful destination for what it creates.

If we expose it first, you can create a mockup-but you still don't have a persistent design entity or clean catalog-creation workflow.

I would instead sequence it:

```text
1. Secure Printful APIs
        ↓
2. Normalize variants
        ↓
3. Protect existing checkout
        ↓
4. Establish storefront-owned product structure
        ↓
5. Establish designs/artwork
        ↓
6. Connect ProductDesigner
        ↓
7. Build catalog/product creator
```

Then the designer becomes a **tool inside your catalog administration system**, rather than a disconnected page.

### Bottom line

The audit validates the architecture document we created, but the situation is considerably better than needing a rebuild.

**Keep the storefront. Keep `products`. Keep `orders`. Keep Stripe. Keep the Printful Edge Functions. Keep the new Printful API layer. Keep the Product Designer.**

The next implementation should primarily change the relationship:

```text

Printful

TARGET

Store Variant UUID
   ↓
Cart
   ↓
Provider Mapping
   ↓
Printful Variant ID
   ↓
Printful
```

That is the critical Phase 2 foundation. After that, we can safely layer the **storefront-owned catalog + reusable design library + automated product/mockup builder** on top without fighting the old Printify architecture.

## What comes next

The next phase should be the **Storefront Catalog Foundation**, and this is where the project starts becoming the architecture we originally discussed.

Importantly, we're **not** going to make “sync more Printful products” the catalog strategy.

Printful becomes the manufacturing layer beneath that catalog:

```text

   ↓

   ↓

   ↓

   ↓

```

That distinction is especially important now because your database is clean. We don't need to design around old Printify demo data anymore.

### I would divide the Catalog work into three smaller phases

**Catalog Foundation** should come first: storefront-owned product fields, slugs/SEO, publication controls, proper variant administration, and the admin product-management foundation.

Then **Design & Mockup Catalog** should introduce reusable designs, artwork records, product/design relationships, generated mockups and persistent product imagery.

Finally **Catalog Builder** can combine a Printful blank product + your design + selected variants + pricing + mockups and publish the resulting commercial product to your storefront.

That eventually gives you the workflow we originally wanted:

```text
Choose Printful blank
        ↓
Choose design
        ↓
Choose colors/sizes
        ↓
Set retail prices
        ↓
Generate mockups
        ↓
Review
        ↓
PUBLISH
        ↓
Your storefront product
```

And later the same architecture can support another provider without redesigning your storefront.

**The next prompt should therefore be “Storefront Catalog Foundation,” not another Printful prompt.** I recommend we keep it scoped just as tightly as Phase 2: build the commercial catalog foundation first, and deliberately leave designs/mockups/catalog-builder functionality for the following phase.

without requiring Printful to be the source of truth for those relationships.

# IMPORTANT DISTINCTION

There are THREE different objects.

## 1. DESIGN

Reusable creative artwork.

Example:

```text
"Cook County Heritage"
```

Stored once.

May be used on many products.

---

## 2. PRODUCT DESIGN

Relationship between a design and a commercial storefront product.

Example:

```text
Cook County Heritage
        +
Premium T-Shirt
        +
Front placement
        +
DTG
```

---

## 3. MOCKUP

Rendered product image created from the relationship.

Example:

```text
Black Premium T-Shirt
with
Cook County Heritage
printed on front
```

These must NOT be represented as the same database object.

---

# OUT OF SCOPE

DO NOT build the full Catalog Builder yet.

Specifically DO NOT implement:

```text
automatic storefront product creation from Printful blanks
bulk product generation
county-by-county product generation
automatic publishing
customer-facing designer
customer artwork customization
multi-provider rendering
Printify support
Mockup Generator v2 migration
bulk design automation
AI artwork generation
collections
product bundles
automated SEO generation
mass publishing
```

Those belong to later phases.

This phase creates the persistent asset/design/mockup foundation required by those capabilities.

---

# STEP 0 — PRE-IMPLEMENTATION INSPECTION

Before modifying anything, inspect the CURRENT repository.

Verify:

```text
products
product_variants
categories

src/lib/catalog/
src/lib/printful/

src/components/product-designer/

src/app/api/printful/artwork-upload
src/app/api/printful/mockups
src/app/api/printful/mockups/[taskKey]
src/app/api/printful/mockups/persist

Supabase Storage usage
store-images bucket

admin product management
existing image handling

all active migrations
```

Determine exactly what Phase 1 already implemented.

DO NOT duplicate:

```text
Printful client
Mockup API client
template API client
artwork upload endpoint
mockup persistence endpoint
polling infrastructure
Product Designer components
```

Reuse them.

---

# STEP 1 — VERIFY CURRENT STORAGE

Inspect the existing:

```text
store-images
```

Supabase Storage bucket.

Determine:

```text
current folders
upload policies
read policies
admin write access
public/private behavior
existing artwork paths
existing mockup paths
```

The earlier architecture used concepts similar to:

```text
store-images/artwork/
store-images/mockups/
```

Verify actual behavior.

Do not create duplicate buckets unless there is a compelling reason.

---

# STEP 2 — CREATE DESIGNS TABLE

Create a new migration.

Add:

```text
designs
```

Conceptual schema:

```text
id                  uuid primary key

name                text not null
slug                text
description         text

artwork_url         text not null
storage_path        text

file_name           text
file_type           text
file_size           bigint

width               integer
height              integer

status              text
tags                text[]

created_by          uuid nullable

created_at          timestamptz
updated_at          timestamptz
```

Adapt to existing project conventions.

Do not add fields merely because they appear in this conceptual example.

---

# STEP 3 — DESIGN IDENTITY

The canonical design identity must be:

```text
designs.id UUID
```

NOT:

```text
filename
artwork URL
Printful file ID
storage path
slug
```

This allows the underlying artwork file to be replaced without changing the logical design identity.

---

# STEP 4 — DESIGN STATUS

Use a small lifecycle.

Preferred:

```text
active
archived
```

Draft may be added only if useful.

Do not physically delete a design that is referenced by products unless explicitly safe.

---

# STEP 5 — DESIGN SLUG

If useful for administration, support a stable design slug.

Example:

```text
cook-county-heritage
```

It does not need to become a public route in this phase.

Use the existing slug utility if appropriate rather than creating another incompatible implementation.

---

# STEP 6 — ARTWORK STORAGE

Artwork files must persist in Supabase Storage.

Preferred conceptual path:

```text
store-images/
    artwork/
        <design-uuid>/
            original.png
```

or equivalent.

Avoid relying permanently on arbitrary filenames.

The database should retain:

```text
design ID
storage path
usable URL
metadata
```

---

# STEP 7 — DO NOT STORE IMAGE BYTES IN POSTGRES

PostgreSQL stores metadata and relationships.

Supabase Storage stores actual artwork files.

Do NOT store:

```text
base64 images
binary PNG data
large image blobs
```

inside the designs table.

---

# STEP 8 — ARTWORK UPLOAD INTEGRATION

Reuse:

```text
/api/printful/artwork-upload
```

where appropriate.

However, separate these concepts:

```text
STORE ARTWORK PERSISTENCE
```

from:

```text
PRINTFUL ARTWORK USAGE
```

Uploading artwork into the storefront should create/persist a design independently of whether Printful is immediately called.

---

# STEP 9 — DESIGN CREATION WORKFLOW

Admin workflow:

```text
Upload artwork
      ↓
Supabase Storage
      ↓
Create design record
      ↓
Design receives UUID
      ↓
Available in Design Library
```

Printful should not be required merely to create a design.

---

# STEP 10 — FILE VALIDATION

Validate uploads server-side.

At minimum evaluate:

```text
allowed MIME types
maximum file size
non-empty file
valid image type
```

Likely supported formats should follow actual Printful requirements and existing application capabilities.

Do NOT invent broad file support.

Preserve transparency for PNG artwork.

Do not unnecessarily recompress source artwork.

---

# STEP 11 — STORAGE SECURITY

Design creation/upload is ADMIN functionality.

Use existing:

```text
requireAdmin()
```

for relevant Next.js mutations.

Do not expose unrestricted public uploads.

Review Storage policies as well as API authentication.

API authorization alone does not replace Storage policy review.

---

# STEP 12 — CREATE PRODUCT_DESIGNS TABLE

Create:

```text
product_designs
```

This represents:

```text
STORE PRODUCT
      +
DESIGN
      +
PRINT CONFIGURATION
```

Conceptual schema:

```text
id                    uuid primary key

product_id            uuid not null
design_id             uuid not null

provider              text
placement             text
technique             text

printfile_id          text nullable

configuration         jsonb

is_primary            boolean

created_at            timestamptz
updated_at            timestamptz
```

Adapt to actual Printful data requirements.

---

# STEP 13 — PRODUCT_DESIGNS FOREIGN KEYS

Establish:

```text
product_designs.product_id
        ↓
products.id

product_designs.design_id
        ↓
designs.id
```

Use safe deletion behavior.

A product/design relationship should not accidentally destroy:

```text
product
design
order history
```

---

# STEP 14 — DESIGN REUSE

A design must support:

```text
ONE DESIGN
     ↓
MANY PRODUCT_DESIGNS
     ↓
MANY PRODUCTS
```

Example:

```text
Cook County Design
      │
      ├── T-Shirt
      ├── Hoodie
      ├── Sweatshirt
      └── Mug
```

Do NOT duplicate the artwork file for every product.

---

# STEP 15 — MULTIPLE DESIGNS PER PRODUCT

The schema must also permit:

```text
ONE PRODUCT
     ↓
MULTIPLE PRODUCT_DESIGNS
```

This allows future use cases such as:

```text
front design
back design
left sleeve
right sleeve
embroidery location
```

Do not assume exactly one design per product.

---

# STEP 16 — PLACEMENT

Store placement on:

```text
product_designs
```

not globally on:

```text
designs
```

because the same design can have different placements on different products.

Examples may include:

```text
front
back
left
right
sleeve
```

but do not hard-code a universal placement list if Printful returns provider-specific placement data.

---

# STEP 17 — TECHNIQUE

Store technique at the product-design relationship level.

Examples:

```text
DTG
embroidery
DTF
sublimation
```

Do not assume every Printful product supports every technique.

Use actual provider capabilities.

---

# STEP 18 — PRINTFILE / TEMPLATE INFORMATION

Phase 1 already implemented Printful:

```text
printfiles
layout templates
techniques
placements
```

Reuse those services.

Store only the provider configuration necessary to reproduce the design placement.

Do not duplicate the entire Printful catalog response into PostgreSQL.

---

# STEP 19 — DESIGN CONFIGURATION

Use:

```text
product_designs.configuration JSONB
```

or an equivalent structure for placement-specific information that does not deserve dedicated columns yet.

Possible information:

```text
position
scale
rotation
print area
template dimensions
source dimensions
```

Use actual existing Product Designer output.

Do not invent configuration fields that the designer does not produce.

---

# STEP 20 — CONFIGURATION VERSIONING

Include a lightweight configuration version if needed.

Example:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "..."
}
```

This can help later if Product Designer output evolves.

Do not build a complex versioning system.

---

# STEP 21 — CREATE PRODUCT_IMAGES TABLE

Normalize persistent storefront product imagery.

Create:

```text
product_images
```

Conceptual schema:

```text
id                  uuid primary key

product_id          uuid not null
product_variant_id  uuid nullable

source              text

storage_path        text
image_url           text not null

alt_text            text

is_primary          boolean
display_order       integer

mockup_task_key     text nullable

created_at          timestamptz
updated_at          timestamptz
```

Use actual project conventions.

---

# STEP 22 — IMAGE SOURCE

Support an image source classification such as:

```text
printful_mockup
manual
provider
```

Keep it simple.

Do not build a generalized DAM taxonomy.

The purpose is to know where a storefront image originated.

---

# STEP 23 — PRODUCT IMAGE OWNERSHIP

The storefront owns the persistent image record.

Printful-generated image URLs must not be the long-term storefront dependency.

Desired:

```text
Printful temporary/generated URL
          ↓
download/persist
          ↓
Supabase Storage
          ↓
product_images
          ↓
storefront
```

---

# STEP 24 — PRODUCT_IMAGES RELATIONSHIPS

Required:

```text
product_images.product_id
        ↓
products.id
```

Optional variant association:

```text
product_images.product_variant_id
        ↓
product_variants.id
```

This allows a mockup to represent:

```text
Black / M
```

or a broader product image with no specific variant.

---

# STEP 25 — PRIMARY IMAGE

Enforce sane primary-image behavior.

A product should have at most one primary image under the chosen model.

If strict DB enforcement is awkward because of partial conditions, use a safe transactional/application mechanism and document it.

Do not allow multiple competing primary images accidentally.

---

# STEP 26 — IMAGE ORDER

Support:

```text
display_order
```

so admins can control storefront image order.

Do not depend on creation timestamps for merchandising order.

---

# STEP 27 — ALT TEXT

Support store-owned:

```text
alt_text
```

Do not simply use filenames as alt text.

Provide sensible fallback behavior from:

```text
product title
+
variant/color where appropriate
```

---

# STEP 28 — EXISTING products.images JSONB

DO NOT immediately remove:

```text
products.images
```

Use a transition approach.

Initially:

```text
product_images
      ↓
preferred

products.images
      ↓
fallback
```

Once the new image system is proven, a later migration can retire JSONB.

---

# STEP 29 — EXISTING PRINTFUL CDN IMAGES

Do not break existing products.

Existing Printful CDN images may remain as fallback during transition.

Do not attempt an uncontrolled bulk download unless specifically necessary.

---

# STEP 30 — MOCKUP GENERATION WORKFLOW

Connect the existing Phase 1 mockup infrastructure to persistent catalog records.

Desired admin flow:

```text
Select product
      ↓
Select design
      ↓
Select placement
      ↓
Select technique
      ↓
Configure design
      ↓
Generate mockup
      ↓
Printful async task
      ↓
Poll task
      ↓
Mockup complete
      ↓
Persist image
      ↓
Create product_images row
```

---

# STEP 31 — DO NOT REBUILD MOCKUP API

Reuse:

```text
POST /api/printful/mockups
GET /api/printful/mockups/[taskKey]
POST /api/printful/mockups/persist
```

Modify only what is necessary to connect them to:

```text
designs
product_designs
product_images
```

---

# STEP 32 — MOCKUP TASK PERSISTENCE

Evaluate whether mockup jobs need persistent tracking.

If useful, create:

```text
mockup_tasks
```

Conceptual schema:

```text
id
product_id
product_design_id

provider
provider_task_key

status

error_message

created_at
completed_at
```

Possible statuses:

```text
pending
processing
completed
failed
```

Create this table ONLY if it materially improves recovery/administration over the existing client-side polling.

Given that mockup generation is asynchronous, persistent task tracking is preferred if implementation remains straightforward.

---

# STEP 33 — ASYNC SAFETY

Mockup generation must handle:

```text
pending
processing
completed
failed
timeout
```

Do not assume a task finishes on the first poll.

Do not create infinite polling.

Use the existing polling behavior where sound.

---

# STEP 34 — PERSIST COMPLETED MOCKUPS

Phase 1 already implemented:

```text
persistGeneratedMockups()
```

Reuse it.

Completed mockups should be copied to Supabase Storage.

Do not leave the storefront dependent on temporary Printful URLs.

---

# STEP 35 — CONNECT MOCKUP TO PRODUCT

After persistence, create a:

```text
product_images
```

record.

The record should identify:

```text
product
optional variant
storage path
persistent URL
source = printful_mockup
mockup task if tracked
display order
primary state
```

---

# STEP 36 — MOCKUP DEDUPLICATION

Avoid creating duplicate product image rows when the same completed mockup is persisted more than once.

Use an appropriate stable relationship such as:

```text
mockup task
+
source image
+
product
```

or another deterministic mechanism supported by the actual implementation.

Do not rely solely on filename.

---

# STEP 37 — MOCKUP FAILURE

A failed mockup task must NOT:

```text
delete product
delete design
delete product_design
remove existing images
```

Store/report the failure and allow retry.

---

# STEP 38 — DESIGN LIBRARY ADMIN PAGE

Create an admin-only Design Library.

Use existing admin UI conventions.

Suggested route:

```text
/admin/designs
```

unless repository conventions indicate a better route.

Display:

```text
Artwork thumbnail
Design name
Status
Usage count
Created
Updated
```

Do not overload the initial page.

---

# STEP 39 — DESIGN CREATION

Admin should be able to:

```text
Upload artwork
Name design
Add description
Add optional tags
Save
```

After saving:

```text
design record exists
artwork persists
design appears in library
```

No Printful product relationship is required yet.

---

# STEP 40 — DESIGN EDITING

Admin may edit:

```text
name
description
tags
status
```

Do not automatically replace artwork simply because metadata changes.

Artwork replacement should be an explicit action.

---

# STEP 41 — DESIGN ARCHIVING

Prefer:

```text
status = archived
```

instead of deleting designs used by products.

Archived designs should remain available to existing product relationships but should not normally appear in new-design selection.

---

# STEP 42 — DESIGN USAGE

Show where a design is used.

Example:

```text
Cook County Heritage

Used on:
2 products
```

A detailed relationship view is useful if easy to implement.

Do not build analytics.

---

# STEP 43 — PRODUCT ADMIN INTEGRATION

Extend the existing admin product editor with a section such as:

```text
DESIGNS & MOCKUPS
```

It should allow:

```text
view attached designs
attach design
configure placement
configure technique
generate mockup
view generated mockups
select primary image
```

Use existing UI patterns.

Do not redesign the entire product editor.

---

# STEP 44 — PRODUCT DESIGNER INTEGRATION

The existing:

```text
src/components/product-designer/
```

can now be integrated into the admin workflow.

IMPORTANT:

The Product Designer should no longer produce only transient state.

When the admin saves:

```text
product
+
design
+
configuration
```

persist that configuration to:

```text
product_designs
```

---

# STEP 45 — PRODUCT DESIGNER SCOPE

Keep the designer ADMIN-ONLY.

Do NOT expose it to customers.

Customer personalization is a separate future feature.

---

# STEP 46 — DESIGNER AUTHORIZATION

All designer-related API operations must require:

```text
requireAdmin()
```

or the established admin authorization equivalent.

Do not rely on hidden routes for security.

---

# STEP 47 — PRODUCT / PRINTFUL COMPATIBILITY

Before generating a mockup, verify the storefront product has a valid Printful provider mapping.

Conceptually:

```text
products.printful_id
```

must identify the underlying provider product.

If no Printful mapping exists:

```text
Mockup generation unavailable
```

Do not guess a provider product.

---

# STEP 48 — VARIANT COMPATIBILITY

Use:

```text
product_variants
```

and their provider mappings.

Do not pass store UUIDs directly to Printful.

Resolve:

```text
store variant UUID
      ↓
printful_variant_id
```

server-side.

---

# STEP 49 — TECHNIQUE COMPATIBILITY

Do not allow unsupported technique/product combinations.

Use actual Printful API capability information from the Phase 1 service layer.

Do not hard-code assumptions such as:

```text
all shirts = DTG
```

---

# STEP 50 — PLACEMENT COMPATIBILITY

Likewise, available placements must come from actual Printful product/template information where possible.

Do not assume:

```text
front
back
```

are universally valid.

---

# STEP 51 — TEMPLATE INFORMATION

Use existing Printful layout-template information to position artwork correctly.

Do not hard-code:

```text
canvas dimensions
print area
offset
template dimensions
```

per product.

---

# STEP 52 — STORE DESIGN CONFIGURATION

Persist enough configuration to regenerate the mockup later.

This is important.

The relationship should survive:

```text
browser refresh
logout
server restart
Printful temporary mockup URL expiration
```

---

# STEP 53 — PRODUCT IMAGE QUERY LAYER

Extend:

```text
src/lib/catalog/
```

with appropriate product-image queries.

Possible:

```text
images.ts
```

Functions may include:

```text
getProductImages()
getPrimaryProductImage()
```

Follow existing architecture.

---

# STEP 54 — UPDATE getPrimaryImage()

The Phase 3 catalog foundation already created:

```text
getPrimaryImage()
```

Update it carefully.

Desired priority:

```text
product_images.is_primary
        ↓
first ordered product_images row
        ↓
legacy products.images
        ↓
safe placeholder
```

Maintain backward compatibility.

---

# STEP 55 — PUBLIC PRODUCT PAGE

Update public product pages to use normalized:

```text
product_images
```

when available.

Preserve existing gallery behavior.

Do not redesign the product page unless required.

---

# STEP 56 — PRODUCT CARDS

Product cards should also prefer the normalized primary product image.

Fallback to existing imagery.

No broken images should result from this migration.

---

# STEP 57 — OPEN GRAPH IMAGES

Phase 3 added SEO metadata.

Update Open Graph product imagery to use the normalized primary storefront image when available.

Fallback safely.

---

# STEP 58 — IMAGE DELETION

Deleting a product image record should be deliberate.

If the corresponding Storage object is exclusively owned by that image record, clean it up safely.

If an asset may be shared:

DO NOT delete the underlying file automatically.

Avoid orphan files where practical.

---

# STEP 59 — DESIGN ARTWORK REPLACEMENT

If artwork is replaced:

```text
designs.id
```

must remain unchanged.

Existing:

```text
product_designs
```

relationships remain valid.

Mark existing mockups as potentially stale if appropriate.

Do not automatically regenerate every mockup in this phase.

---

# STEP 60 — STALE MOCKUP CONCEPT

Provide a simple mechanism to know that a product mockup may need regeneration after:

```text
artwork replacement
placement change
technique change
configuration change
```

This may be:

```text
updated_at comparison
status
needs_regeneration boolean
```

Choose the simplest reliable approach.

Do not build a job queue solely for this.

---

# STEP 61 — RLS FOR DESIGNS

Design records are administrative assets.

Default expectation:

```text
public:
no direct design-table access required

authenticated non-admin:
no mutation

admin:
SELECT
INSERT
UPDATE
DELETE/archive as permitted
```

Use existing admin architecture.

Do not expose the entire design library publicly merely because artwork appears on products.

---

# STEP 62 — RLS FOR PRODUCT_DESIGNS

Treat configuration as internal/admin data unless the public storefront specifically needs it.

Public customers generally do not need:

```text
Printful placement
printfile ID
designer coordinates
internal configuration
```

Do not expose unnecessary implementation details.

---

# STEP 63 — RLS FOR PRODUCT_IMAGES

Published product imagery must be readable by public storefront users.

Admin users can manage it.

Apply RLS consistent with product publication rules where feasible.

Do not accidentally expose images for private/draft products through unrestricted database queries if avoidable.

---

# STEP 64 — STORAGE POLICY REVIEW

Review Storage policies separately.

Verify:

```text
public product images readable as intended
artwork upload admin-only
mockup persistence admin-only
unauthorized deletion prohibited
```

Do not assume table RLS protects Storage objects.

---

# STEP 65 — DO NOT EXPOSE PROVIDER SECRETS

Never expose:

```text
PRINTFUL_API_TOKEN
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY
Stripe secret keys
```

to browser code.

Printful API operations requiring credentials remain server-side.

---

# STEP 66 — TYPES

Add clean storefront types such as:

```text
Design
ProductDesign
ProductImage
MockupTask
```

where appropriate.

Keep them separate from:

```text
PrintfulProduct
PrintfulVariant
PrintfulMockupResponse
```

Do not mix provider DTOs with storefront database entities.

---

# STEP 67 — ERROR HANDLING

Use clear typed errors where practical.

Distinguish:

```text
invalid design
missing provider mapping
unsupported placement
unsupported technique
Printful API failure
mockup timeout
Storage persistence failure
database persistence failure
```

Do not expose secrets or raw provider internals to public users.

Admin errors may be more descriptive.

---

# STEP 68 — TRANSACTION / CONSISTENCY SAFETY

Consider failure order.

Example:

```text
Printful mockup succeeds
        ↓
Storage copy succeeds
        ↓
DB insert fails
```

Do not silently report full success.

Return a recoverable error and avoid unnecessary duplicate files on retry where practical.

Likewise:

```text
Storage upload succeeds
        ↓
design DB creation fails
```

clean up the newly uploaded orphan when safe.

---

# STEP 69 — DO NOT MODIFY PHASE 2 COMMERCE IDENTITY

Preserve:

```text
products.id
product_variants.id
CartItem.variant_id
```

Do not change the checkout identity model.

---

# STEP 70 — DO NOT MODIFY FULFILLMENT UNNECESSARILY

This phase should not require redesigning:

```text
stripe-checkout
stripe-webhook
printful-webhook
```

If changes become necessary, STOP and explain why before modifying the proven fulfillment architecture.

---

# STEP 71 — PRINTFUL SYNC OWNERSHIP

Preserve Phase 3 behavior:

```text
Store-owned content
        ↓
not overwritten by sync

Provider-owned data
        ↓
refreshed by sync
```

Printful synchronization must not delete:

```text
designs
product_designs
product_images
```

Run:

Do not:

# FINAL ARCHITECTURAL RULE

After Phase 4, this statement must be true:

> The storefront owns the design, its artwork, its relationship to a commercial product, and the persistent product imagery. Printful is used to determine compatible manufacturing configuration and to render mockups, but Printful is not the permanent source of truth for the creative assets or storefront presentation.

Do not begin the Catalog Builder phase during this task.

This phase is the bridge between the infrastructure you've already built and the eventual product-generation system. Once it passes, the next phase can finally be the **Catalog Builder**—select a Printful blank, select one of your stored designs, select variants/placement, set pricing, generate mockups, and create a draft storefront product from that combination.

The best use of your time is **preparing manufacturing-ready products and artwork**, rather than building out your commercial storefront inside Printful. Printful's current documentation confirms that product templates are reusable product/design configurations and aren't tied to a specific store; they can later be published to a store. I would do these things:

1. **Upload your real designs to Printful.** Use the Design Maker to check whether each artwork file fits correctly, has sufficient quality, and works with the printing technique you intend to use. Printful's Design Maker exposes the techniques and product-specific design requirements. ([Printful Help Center](https://help.printful.com/hc/en-us/articles/50264179910673-How-does-the-Design-Maker-work?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

2. **Experiment with blank products.** Identify the shirts, hoodies, sweatshirts, hats, etc. that you actually want your storefront to offer. Pay attention to available colors, sizes, techniques, print areas and costs. You don't need to turn all of them into live store products yet.

3. **Create Product Templates.** This is probably the most valuable thing you can do right now. For example:

```text

        +
Bella+Canvas Shirt
        +
Black / White / Navy
        +
Front DTG
        =
Printful Product Template
```

Templates can hold the product, print file and relevant color/size configuration without forcing you to establish your storefront pricing or description yet. ([Printful Help Center](https://help.printful.com/hc/en-us/articles/50263591495185-What-s-a-product-template-and-how-does-it-work?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

4. **Test different placements and techniques.** For example, compare front-center DTG, left-chest, back print, embroidery, and other supported placements. This work will be useful when Phase 4 begins storing `placement`, `technique`, and configuration in `product_designs`.

5. **Generate and inspect mockups.** Look at which Printful mockup styles you actually want customers to see. Printful lets you choose main/additional mockups and download generated mockups. ([Printful Help Center](https://help.printful.com/hc/en-us/articles/50264186389393-What-are-mockup-images?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This will help us later decide which mockups your Catalog Builder should request automatically.

6. **Order a sample of the products you're serious about.** If your account is eligible, Printful currently offers sample orders at a discount; Printful says these are intended for checking product/print quality and creating content, not resale. ([Printful Help Center](https://help.printful.com/hc/en-us/articles/50261041946001-How-do-sample-orders-work?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) This is especially worthwhile before building a large catalog around a particular garment.

If live verification discovers a SMALL, CLEAR defect directly within Phase 4 functionality, you may fix it.


2. Make the smallest safe change.
3. Add/update regression test.
4. Rerun affected test.
5. Rerun complete regression.
6. Document the change.

# PROBLEM TO SOLVE

The storefront currently stores:

```text
products.printful_id = 476330305
```

which is the Printful STORE/SYNC product ID.

However, Printful Mockup Generator functionality requires:

```text
Printful CATALOG product ID = 903
```

Phase 4 currently resolves/stores this indirectly.

That is functional but creates an unnecessary runtime dependency:

```text
Store Product UUID
      ↓
products.printful_id
      ↓
Printful /store/products/{sync_id}
```
