## Response:
gpt-5-6

Yes. Since this will be your **first real production item**, I would create a **new production-quality design specifically for the test**, rather than reusing the old Phase 5.2 artwork. Your report says that artwork came from earlier embroidery/mockup testing and still needs production-quality verification. `PHASE-6-PRODUCTION-READINESS-AND-LAUNCH-HARDENING-REPORT.md`

For the first product, I'd keep it simple: use the **Bella+Canvas 3001 T-shirt** you've already validated technically, with a black shirt, front DTG placement, and one strong graphic. That lets Phase 7 test a product/variant path your system already understands instead of introducing a new blank at the same time.

For **CountyBuys**, I'd make the design broadly sellable rather than geographic. Some directions that fit the marketplace concept are: family humor, Gen-X/80s-90s nostalgia, dad/grandpa humor, motivational/cultural statements, profession/lifestyle humor, or a clever everyday statement. For the first test, something visually strong but not overly complicated is ideal-large readable typography plus a simple graphic element. Avoid tiny text and intricate details because we want the physical print to tell us clearly whether sizing, placement, sharpness, color, and DTG quality are correct.

For example, we could create an original design around a concept like:

> **STILL ORIGINAL**  
> *They don't make 'em like this anymore.*

That could work as a general Gen-X/older-generation lifestyle design without putting a county name on anybody's chest. 😄 It could later expand naturally to a sweatshirt, hoodie, mug, hat variation, etc.

And **yes, I recommend creating the actual image now**. Not merely a mockup-the **production artwork** that will ultimately be sent to Printful. We can deliberately create it for DTG with a transparent background, strong contrast for a black shirt, a print-friendly composition, and enough resolution for the intended print area.

Then the sequence becomes:

**create production artwork → inspect its actual dimensions/format → add it as a real Design in your system → generate the storefront mockup → let Phase 7A validate it → order that exact shirt.**

If you want, I can create the **“STILL ORIGINAL - They don't make 'em like this anymore”** production design now, or we can choose a different first-product concept.

## Prompt:
why a live key needed?

## Response:
gpt-5-6

Because **Phase 7 was defined as the first real production transaction**. A Stripe live key is needed only for the **real-payment portion** of that test.

Your application has already proven the complete workflow using Stripe **test mode** in Phase 5.2. Phase 7 is intended to prove that the same system works with an actual payment and production order.

The distinction is:

```text
STRIPE TEST MODE
sk_test_...
      ↓
Test card
      ↓
Test Checkout Session
      ↓
livemode = false
      ↓
Test webhook
      ↓
Local order
      ↓
Printful draft

STRIPE LIVE MODE
sk_live_...
      ↓
Real card/payment
      ↓
Real Checkout Session
      ↓
livemode = true
      ↓
LIVE webhook
      ↓
Real local paid order
      ↓
Real Printful draft
```

### But there is an important distinction

**Printful does not require your Stripe live key.**

Printful and Stripe are separate systems. The Stripe live key is needed because **your storefront uses Stripe to collect the customer's real payment**, not because Printful needs Stripe.

Your architecture is essentially:

```text
Customer
   │
   ▼
Your Storefront
   │
   ├──── Stripe ──── Collect customer payment
   │
   └──── Printful ── Manufacture/fulfill product
```

Your Printful API token is what authorizes your application to create the Printful order.

### Could we test Printful production without Stripe LIVE?

**Yes.**

Technically, we could create a controlled Printful draft directly from the verified product and then manually confirm it. But that would test:

```text
Product
→ fulfillment resolver
→ Printful
→ production
```

It would **not** prove your actual commercial pipeline:

```text
real customer
→ real Stripe payment
→ live Stripe webhook
→ paid local order
→ frozen snapshot
→ Printful order
```

That's why I put Stripe LIVE into Phase 7.

### And we don't have to turn the whole store loose

This is worth emphasizing. We're not saying:

> "Switch Stripe to live and launch CountyBuys."

We're saying:

> "Temporarily/controlledly enable the production payment rail and make exactly one real purchase through the same path a future customer will use."

Your Phase 7C report specifically ended with Stripe still in test mode and said the remaining Phase 7 actions were to configure the live keys and verify the live webhook. `PHASE-7C-PRODUCTION-CANDIDATE-FINALIZATION-REPORT.md`

So **yes, the live key is necessary for the particular Phase 7 test we've designed. It is not necessary to create or test a Printful product by itself.**

And this is exactly why we're stopping before you enter anything: once we cross this boundary, we're testing **real commerce**, not just software.

============================================================
CORE PRINCIPLE
============================================================

A Product Recipe is NOT a product.

A Product Recipe is NOT an order.

A Product Recipe is NOT a Printful Sync Product.

A Product Recipe is a reusable, validated merchandising/manufacturing
template that can produce one or more ProductSpecifications.

Example:

Recipe:

"Standard Graphic Tee"

could define:

Printful catalog product:
Bella+Canvas 3001

Technique:
DTG

Placement:
front

Allowed colors:
Black
Navy
White
Heather Grey

Sizes:
S-3XL

Pricing rule:
base provider cost + configured margin

Mockup views:
front
model
flat

Publication:
draft

A design can then be combined with that recipe to generate a complete
ProductSpecification.

============================================================
ARCHITECTURE
============================================================

Implement:

Design
   +
ProductRecipe
   +
Commercial Inputs
        ↓
Recipe Resolver
        ↓
ProductSpecification
        ↓
validateProductSpecification()
        ↓
dryRunProductSpecification()
        ↓
Product Creation Engine

Recipes MUST NOT bypass ProductSpecification.

Recipes MUST NOT write products directly.

============================================================
AI SAFETY BOUNDARY
============================================================

Future AI merchandising may choose:

recipe

design

title

description

category

collections

pricing strategy

SEO suggestions

But AI must NEVER invent:

Printful catalog product IDs

Printful catalog variant IDs

printfile IDs

unsupported placements

unsupported techniques

Provider IDs must come from validated provider/catalog data.

============================================================
PART 1 - DATABASE MODEL
============================================================

Create normalized recipe persistence.

Preferred table:

product_recipes

Suggested fields:

id uuid primary key

name text

slug text unique

description text

status text
  draft
  active
  archived

  default "printful"

printful_catalog_id integer

technique text

placement text

printfile_id integer nullable

variant_rules jsonb

mockup_rules jsonb

commercial_defaults jsonb

publication_default text

metadata jsonb

created_at

updated_at

Do not store Stripe information.

Do not store order information.

Do not store fulfillment_snapshot.

============================================================
VARIANT RULES
============================================================

Do NOT hardcode store variant UUIDs into recipes.

Recipes operate against provider catalog variants.

Example:

{
  "colors": ["Black", "Navy", "White"],
  "sizes": ["S", "M", "L", "XL", "2XL"],
  "exclude_variant_ids": []
}

The Recipe Resolver validates these rules against current Printful
catalog data.

Store variant UUIDs are created later by the Product Creation Engine.

## Response:
gpt-5-6

Excellent. That closes the one database prerequisite I was concerned about. Your newer verification supersedes the report's earlier "pending migration" state: `product_recipes`, `products.recipe_id`, `products.recipe_version`, and `designs.file_hash` are now present, and the three starter recipes exist as drafts.

The architecture is therefore at the point we designed for: Recipe → `ProductSpecification` → validation → Product Creation Engine. The report confirms that recipes never bypass that specification layer or write products directly. `PHASE-8C-PRODUCT-RECIPE-SYSTEM-REPORT.md` It also confirms the three starter recipes-Premium Long Sleeve, Everyday Graphic Tee, and Embroidered Dad Hat-were intentionally created as drafts and generated no products. `PHASE-8C-PRODUCT-RECIPE-SYSTEM-REPORT.md`

The historical snapshot remains immutable, which is our continuing safety benchmark. `PHASE-8C-PRODUCT-RECIPE-SYSTEM-REPORT.md`

So yes: **Phase 9 is now GO.**

But Phase 9 should not immediately mean "generate hundreds of products." The next milestone should prove **controlled batch generation** first:

```text
Designs
   ×
Recipes
   ↓
Batch Plan
   ↓
Resolve
   ↓
Validate
   ↓
Dry Run
   ↓
Preview
   ↓
Operator Approval
   ↓
Generate as DRAFT
   ↓
Mockup Jobs
   ↓
Review
   ↓
Bulk Publish
```

That gives us the machinery for mass catalog creation without allowing an AI or a batch loop to spray bad products into CountyBuys.

One deliberate change from the previous roadmap: I would **not call Phase 9 "mass generation" yet**. It builds the mass-generation capability, but its acceptance test should remain only **2 designs × 2 recipes = at most four draft products**. Once that passes-including replay/idempotency-we can safely turn the volume up instead of discovering a multiplication bug after creating 300 products.

## Response:
gpt-5-6

Phase 9 is a major milestone. I reviewed the report against your summary. The important architecture is now in place: batch generation orchestrates the existing **Design → Recipe → ProductSpecification → Product Creation Engine** pipeline rather than introducing a second product-creation path. `PHASE-9-BATCH-CATALOG-GENERATOR-REPORT.md`

There are, however, **three things I would close before moving into AI merchandising**. The report calls mockup processing PASS, but the remaining-risks section says the batch mockup pipeline is **not actually wired to Printful**; products currently require mockups to be generated from the individual product workspace. It also says variant availability is still coming from the client instead of being resolved server-side from Printful, and bulk category/collection assignment lacks its API. `PHASE-9-BATCH-CATALOG-GENERATOR-REPORT.md`

So I would **not make AI the next implementation yet**. AI will multiply whatever weaknesses remain in the deterministic pipeline. Let's make Phase 10A the productionization of the Batch Generator, then Phase 10B can introduce AI merchandising.

Also, the test report should not be interpreted as “740/740 PASS”: it explicitly records **four pre-existing failures** involving `crypto.randomUUID()`. `PHASE-9-BATCH-CATALOG-GENERATOR-REPORT.md` Those should finally be cleaned up now.

## Prompt:
what [AI merchandising]?was thta part of the plan, the api,

## Response:
gpt-5-6

Yes - **AI merchandising was part of the longer-term plan, but it was not part of the Printful API itself.** I should have made that distinction clearer.

Your Phase 9 report actually says that the current commercial content is generated deterministically from the design + recipe, and that **“AI enrichment can plug into this layer in Phase 10.”** `PHASE-9-BATCH-CATALOG-GENERATOR-REPORT.md` It also explicitly recommends Phase 10 as **“AI Merchandising & Catalog Expansion”**, including AI-assisted titles, descriptions, SEO, collections, and categories. `PHASE-9-BATCH-CATALOG-GENERATOR-REPORT.md`

### What we originally meant by it

It is a layer **above** the Printful API:

```text
                    COUNTYBUYS
                        │
                AI Merchandising
                        │
          "What should we sell?"
                        │
       ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
       ▼                ▼                ▼
    Designs         Collections       Content
                                      Titles
                                      Descriptions
                                      SEO
                        │
                        ▼
                 Product Recipes
                        │
                        ▼
               Batch Catalog Generator
                        │
                        ▼
              Product Creation Engine
                        │
                        ▼
                  Printful API
                 manufacturing
                 mockups/catalog
                 fulfillment
```

So the responsibilities are deliberately different.

**Printful API:** tells your system *what Printful can manufacture* - products, variants, colors, sizes, techniques, placements, printfiles, mockups and fulfillment.

**Recipe engine:** tells your system *how CountyBuys wants a particular type of product constructed*.

**Batch generator:** safely creates many products from Design × Recipe combinations.

**AI merchandising:** would eventually help decide *what combinations make commercial sense* and write/organize the storefront content.

For example, AI could take a design such as **“Grandpa Still Original”** and suggest that it belongs in *Grand Life*, select the long-sleeve recipe rather than a canvas recipe, propose a storefront title and description, generate SEO copy, and perhaps flag another product/design combination as inappropriate.

But critically, it **cannot invent Printful product IDs, variants, placements, techniques, or manufacturing configuration**. Those stay controlled by your deterministic Recipe/ProductSpecification/Printful API system.

And yes, this was intentional from earlier in the architecture. Phase 8C explicitly established that boundary: provider IDs have to come from validated Printful catalog data rather than being invented by AI or recipes. `PHASE-8C-PRODUCT-RECIPE-SYSTEM-REPORT.md`

### But we don't have to build AI next

This is the important part.

**AI merchandising isn't required for the store to work.** You already have:

```text
Design
   ↓
Recipe
   ↓
ProductSpecification
   ↓
Batch Generator
   ↓
Draft Products
   ↓
Human Review
   ↓
Publish
```

That's a complete deterministic catalog system.

AI was planned as an **optional intelligence layer on top**, so instead of you manually deciding how 100 designs should be named, categorized, described, SEO'd, and matched to appropriate product recipes, an AI agent could propose those decisions for your approval.

So when I said **Phase 10B AI Merchandising**, I wasn't suggesting changing the Printful integration or adding some new Printful AI API. I meant adding an agent to **your CountyBuys platform** that uses the catalog infrastructure we've spent Phases 1-9 building.

For now, I still think **10A should finish the missing deterministic pieces first**-especially real batch mockups and server-side Printful variant validation. The Phase 9 report confirms those are not yet fully connected. `PHASE-9-BATCH-CATALOG-GENERATOR-REPORT.md`

Then we can decide whether you actually want the AI merchandising agent at all, and if so, **which model/API you want powering it**. It doesn't need to be coupled to Printful.

## Response:
gpt-5-6

Yes. And I think we should decide it **before continuing Phase 10A**, because it affects how we design the merchandising hooks now.

My recommendation for CountyBuys is: **yes, include AI merchandising, but make it advisory and approval-based-not autonomous.**

The architecture should be:

```text
DESIGNS
   │
   ▼
AI MERCHANDISING AGENT
   │
   ├── Product suitability
   ├── Recipe recommendations
   ├── Collection recommendations
   ├── Product titles
   ├── Descriptions
   ├── SEO title/description
   ├── Tags / audience
   └── Pricing suggestions
           │
           ▼
     MERCHANDISING PLAN
           │
        HUMAN REVIEW
           │
           ▼
       APPROVED PLAN
           │
           ▼
      Product Recipes
           │
           ▼
     Batch Generator
           │
           ▼
 ProductSpecification
           │
           ▼
 Product Creation Engine
           │
           ▼
       Printful API
```

The AI **does not control Printful**. It never gets to invent catalog IDs, variant IDs, placements, techniques, or printfile IDs. Phase 8C already established that provider IDs must come from validated Printful data. `PHASE-8C-PRODUCT-RECIPE-SYSTEM-REPORT.md`

### What I would let the AI do

For a design such as **Grandpa Still Original**, we could give the agent the available recipes and your CountyBuys merchandising rules. It could return something conceptually like:

```text
Design:
Grandpa Still Original

Recommended:
✓ Premium Long Sleeve Graphic Tee
✓ Everyday Graphic Tee
✓ Mug

Possible:
△ Dad Hat - artwork adaptation required

Do not use:
✗ Canvas

Collections:
Grand Life
Family First
Gifts

Audience:
Grandfathers
Adult children buying gifts
Father's Day shoppers

Suggested title:
Grandpa Still Original Vintage Long Sleeve Tee

Suggested retail description:
...

SEO title:
...

SEO description:
...
```

The important part is that this output is a **proposal**, not a product.

You approve/edit it, and only then does the deterministic system take over.

That fits extremely well with what Phase 9 already built. The report deliberately created a commercial-content layer where recipe defaults and operator overrides are used, and specifically left a place for AI enrichment. `PHASE-9-BATCH-CATALOG-GENERATOR-REPORT.md`

### I would NOT give the AI these powers

The AI should never directly:

- create or alter Printful provider IDs;
- change manufacturing technique or placement outside validated recipe options;
- publish products;
- submit Printful fulfillment orders;
- change historical products or order snapshots;
- activate a recipe that fails provider validation;
- silently generate hundreds of products;
- decide that every design belongs on every blank.

This last one is particularly important for CountyBuys. You've been building actual merchandising rules-e.g. some concepts belong on apparel but not wall art. The AI should **reason over those rules**, not just create Cartesian products.

### Which API?

I would use the **OpenAI API** for the merchandising intelligence and keep Printful exactly where it is.

That gives us three separate systems:

```text
OpenAI API
"What should we sell and how should we present it?"
        │
        ▼
CountyBuys Catalog Engine
"Is this allowed and how exactly is it constructed?"
        │
        ▼
Printful API
"Can this physical product be manufactured?"
```

That separation is much cleaner than embedding AI logic inside the Printful integration.

And I would make the model return **structured JSON**, not free-form instructions. Something along these lines:

```json
{
  "design_id": "...",
  "recommended_recipes": [
    {
      "recipe_id": "...",
      "suitability": "recommended",
      "reason": "Strong apparel fit"
    }
  ],
  "collections": [
    "Grand Life",
    "Gifts"
  ],
  "title": "Grandpa Still Original Vintage Long Sleeve Tee",
  "description": "...",
  "seo_title": "...",
  "seo_description": "...",
  "tags": [
    "grandpa",
    "grandfather gift",
    "family"
  ]
}
```

Then **our server validates every ID in that response** against Supabase before anything reaches the Batch Generator.

### One thing I'd change in the roadmap

I wouldn't call Phase 10B simply "AI Merchandising & Catalog Expansion." I'd make it:

**Phase 10B - CountyBuys Merchandising Agent**

And give it an explicit role:

> Analyze designs against CountyBuys' approved product recipes, collections, merchandising rules, audiences, and brand standards; propose commercially appropriate product combinations and storefront content for human approval.

That becomes an actual reusable agent rather than sprinkling AI calls throughout the codebase.

Later it can become considerably more interesting:

```text
                     MERCHANDISING AGENT
                              │
          ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
          ▼                   ▼                   ▼
     Design Analysis     Catalog Planning    Content Creation
          │                   │                   │
          ▼                   ▼                   ▼
     "What is it?"       "Where does it       "How should we
                          belong?"              sell it?"
          │                   │                   │
          └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                              ▼
                     Merchandising Plan
                              │
                         HUMAN APPROVAL
                              │
                              ▼
                       Batch Generator
```

And eventually the feedback loop can use **your own sales data**:

```text
Published Products
       ↓
Views / Cart / Sales
       ↓
Catalog Performance
       ↓
Merchandising Agent
       ↓
"Family humor tees convert,
 but family humor canvases don't."
       ↓
Future Recommendations
```

That's where AI becomes genuinely valuable rather than just a description writer.

So I would lock in the decision now:

**Yes - CountyBuys will have an AI Merchandising Agent. It will use the OpenAI API, produce structured merchandising proposals, operate above the Recipe/Batch system, and require human approval before product generation or publication.**

Phase **10A remains deterministic production hardening**. Then **10B builds this agent**. That preserves the architecture we've already built instead of changing direction.

Yes. I would make **agent management a first-class admin feature inside CountyBuys**, not bury the model name and prompt in environment variables. That gives you control over cost, behavior, versions, and what the agent is allowed to do.

## What you would manage

I envision an **Admin → AI → Merchandising Agent** page with five areas:

| Area | You control |
|---|---|
| **Agent** | enabled/disabled, model, mode |
| **Instructions** | merchandising rules, brand rules, prohibited combinations |
| **Usage** | requests, input/output tokens, estimated cost |
| **Limits** | daily/monthly budget, per-job limits, batch limits |
| **Versions** | prompt versions, model changes, rollback |

So you wouldn't have to edit code every time you want to change something like:

> Don't recommend Family Laughs designs for canvas.

That becomes a merchandising rule managed in the admin.

### Model management

I would **not hard-code one model**.

Have something like:

```text
Merchandising Agent

Status:       ENABLED

Primary model:
GPT-6.1 Sol

Economy model:
GPT-6 Luna

High-quality model:
GPT-6.1 Sol

Mode:
● Advisory
○ Automatic planning
○ Disabled
```

For CountyBuys, Luna can handle inexpensive repetitive work-tags, straightforward SEO fields, classifications-and Sol can handle more nuanced product/design suitability and complete merchandising plans. Both currently support structured outputs, which is exactly what we want for validated JSON rather than unpredictable prose. ([OpenAI Developers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/compare?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

You could later change models from Admin without rewriting the agent.

## Tokens and cost

Every AI operation should create an internal usage record:

```text
AI Usage

Date          Agent          Operation        Model        Input   Output   Cost
Oct 3 1:15    Merchandising  Analyze design   Luna         1,842     623    $...
Oct 3 1:17    Merchandising  Build plan       Sol          3,104   1,221    $...
Oct 3 1:20    Merchandising  SEO              Luna           892     344    $...
```

OpenAI responses expose usage information, and OpenAI also provides an account Usage Dashboard. ([OpenAI Help Center](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10478918-reviewing-api-usage-and-costs?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

But **CountyBuys should maintain its own ledger too**. That way you can answer much more useful questions:

```text
What did AI cost CountyBuys this month?

Which agent used the tokens?

Which batch used them?

Which design caused the request?

How much AI cost was incurred per generated product?
```

That's more useful than only looking at the provider's overall account bill.

## Put a budget around it

I'd give you controls such as:

```text
AI BUDGET

Monthly budget:              $25.00
Warning threshold:           $15.00
Hard internal cutoff:        $25.00

Maximum per batch:            $2.00
Maximum products per AI run:     25

Current month:

Spent:                        $4.17
Remaining:                   $20.83
```

Separately, OpenAI provides organization/project spend controls and spend alerts. OpenAI distinguishes spend alerts-which notify while traffic continues-from spend limits, which can be used to control monthly API spending. ([OpenAI Developers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/rate-limits?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

I'd therefore use **two layers**:

```text
OpenAI account/project limit
          +
CountyBuys internal AI budget
```

CountyBuys' limit should normally be lower.

## And the costs can be quite low

This is another reason I wouldn't default everything to an expensive model.

As of now, standard short-context pricing listed by OpenAI is:

- GPT-6 Luna: **$0.10/M input, $0.50/M output**
- GPT-6.1 Sol: **$2/M input, $10/M output**
- GPT-6 Astra: **$10/M input, $50/M output** ([OpenAI Developers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/compare?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

For example, a merchandising operation using 5,000 input tokens and producing 2,000 output tokens would be roughly **$0.0015 with Luna** or **$0.03 with Sol**, before any additional tool costs. That means we can reserve the stronger model for decisions where its additional reasoning is actually valuable.

[OpenAI API pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing?tab=suite&utm_source=chatgpt.com)

this concerns me with the model, cost, model chosen, etc.

## Response:
gpt-5-6

That concern is justified. I would **change one part of what I just proposed**: CountyBuys should **not let the agent choose its own model**, and we should not build around assumptions about a particular future model name or price.

The application should treat the model provider as infrastructure that **you configure**, not something the merchandising agent controls.

The safer architecture is:

```text
YOU / ADMIN
    │
    ├── Provider: OpenAI
    ├── Model: [you select]
    ├── Max cost/request
    ├── Monthly budget
    ├── Max output tokens
    └── Agent enabled/disabled
              │
              ▼
      Merchandising Agent
              │
              ▼
       Structured proposal
              │
              ▼
        Human approval
```

The agent gets **zero authority to change provider, model, token limits, or budget**.

More importantly, I would not design CountyBuys around `"GPT-X"` scattered throughout the code. We'd create a configuration such as:

```text
AI Provider
OpenAI

Model
[configured model ID]

Max output tokens
2,000

Maximum AI requests per batch
20

Maximum estimated batch cost
$1.00

Monthly CountyBuys budget
$20.00

On budget exceeded
STOP
```

The actual model ID would live in configuration. If six months later you decide a different model has a better cost/quality ratio, you change one setting.

### I also wouldn't let the model determine how many calls it makes

This is particularly important.

We should avoid an open-ended "agent loop" that can repeatedly call the model:

```text
AI thinks
 ↓
calls AI again
 ↓
calls AI again
 ↓
tries something
 ↓
calls AI again...
```

That can make costs difficult to predict.

For CountyBuys, I favor a **bounded AI workflow**:

```text
20 designs
      ↓
ONE merchandising request
(or known-size chunks)
      ↓
structured response
      ↓
validate
      ↓
DONE
```

If we decide it requires two calls, then it is **exactly two calls**, not "however many the agent thinks it needs."

That changes this from an unpredictable autonomous agent into a controlled merchandising service.

### Tokens should have hard ceilings

Each request should have something equivalent to:

```text
Input budget
      ↓
Maximum context size we send

Output budget
      ↓
Maximum response tokens

Request budget
      ↓
Maximum requests/job

Dollar budget
      ↓
Maximum estimated spend/job
```

If any limit is reached:

```text
STOP
```

Not:

```text
Use a cheaper model automatically
```

I wouldn't automatically switch models either. That can produce different behavior without you knowing why.

Instead:

> Batch stopped because AI budget was reached.  
> 14 of 20 designs analyzed.  
> Estimated spend: $0.93 / $1.00 limit.  
> Continue?

**You decide.**

### Model selection should be explicit

I'd make the admin configuration more like:

```text
AI → Provider Configuration

Provider
OpenAI

Model
[select from approved models]

Status
ACTIVE

────────────────────────

Limits

Max output tokens/request      2,000
Max requests/job                  10
Max estimated cost/job         $1.00
Monthly budget                $20.00

────────────────────────

Automatic model switching

OFF

Automatic budget increase

OFF

Agent may change model

NO

Agent may publish products

NO
```

This is substantially safer than the setup I described previously.

### And don't trust our stored price forever

This is another issue.

Model prices change. Models appear and disappear. So we shouldn't write business logic such as:

```ts
if (model === "xyz") {
   cost = tokens * 0.000002;
}
```

and assume it remains correct indefinitely.

I'd separate **usage accounting** from **estimated cost**:

```text
Provider: OpenAI
Model: <actual model ID>
Input tokens: 14,271
Cached input tokens: ...
Output tokens: 3,412
Request ID: ...
Timestamp: ...
```

Those are factual usage records.

Then:

```text
Estimated cost: $X
Pricing version: 2026-10-03
```

is calculated using a separately managed pricing configuration.

That means you can update pricing without changing historical token counts.

### You should be able to turn AI completely off

This may be the most important design requirement.

CountyBuys must continue operating normally with:

```text
AI_ENABLED=false
```

You would still have:

```text
Designs
   ↓
Product Recipes
   ↓
Batch Generator
   ↓
ProductSpecification
   ↓
Draft Products
   ↓
Human merchandising
   ↓
Publish
```

AI simply improves:

```text
title
description
SEO
collection selection
product suitability
tags
```

It should never become a dependency of your catalog engine.

Your Phase 9 architecture already supports that separation because commercial content currently works without AI; the report says it uses design/recipe information and operator overrides, with AI merely envisioned as a later enrichment layer. `PHASE-9-BATCH-CATALOG-GENERATOR-REPORT.md`

### So I'd simplify the roadmap

I would **not build a giant multi-agent management platform yet**. That's premature for CountyBuys.

Instead:

```text
PHASE 10A
Finish deterministic batch production
        ↓
PHASE 10B
Controlled AI Infrastructure
        ↓
PHASE 10C
Merchandising Assistant
```

And 10B can be small:

```text
ai_config
ai_usage
ai_runs
ai_prompt_versions
```

That's enough.

Then the first AI experiment might literally be:

> Take these 5 designs and these 3 approved recipes. Recommend appropriate combinations, collections, titles and descriptions. Return JSON only.

We record exactly how many tokens it used and what it cost.

If it costs $0.03 and produces useful results, great.

If it costs $3 and the recommendations aren't good enough, **turn it off or change the model**.

Nothing else in CountyBuys changes.

So I would make this a hard architectural rule now:

> **AI is optional, bounded, metered, model-pinned, budget-limited, human-approved, and replaceable. The deterministic CountyBuys catalog system must operate fully without it.**

That gives you control over precisely the things you're concerned about: **which model is being used, how often it's called, how many tokens it consumes, what it costs, and whether it's worth continuing to use.**

## Prompt:
Phase 10A.3 — Complete
939/939 tests | TypeScript: 0 errors | Build: PASS | 33/33 live DB checks PASS

1. Root cause — HTML-vs-JSON artwork error
DesignTab.handleFileChange called res.json() unconditionally after fetch("/api/printful/artwork-upload"). When the server returns any non-JSON response (unhandled Next.js error page, proxy error, or session edge case), the browser receives text/html and .json() throws Unexpected token '<'. The fix checks Content-Type: application/json before calling .json() and throws a clean user-facing message instead. Same guard added to handleRegenerateMockups.

2. Files changed
File	Change
src/lib/printful/identity.ts	Catalog Builder path: when printful_id=null but printful_catalog_id is set, return catalog ID directly. No sync product required.
src/app/admin/products/[id]/tabs/DesignTab.tsx	Check Content-Type before .json() on upload and mockup regen. Pass frozen position from configuration to mockup regen payload.
src/__tests__/fulfillment/phase10a3.test.ts	37 new regression tests.
3. Root cause — incorrect printful_id dependency
resolvePrintfulProductIdentity() in identity.ts threw "Product has no Printful sync ID (printful_id is null)" at line 57 — before it ever checked printful_catalog_id. It was written for the legacy Printful Sync model where printful_id is always present. Catalog Builder products deliberately have printful_id=null.

4. How Catalog Builder mockup regeneration now resolves catalog identity
resolvePrintfulProductIdentity() now checks printful_id first. If null, it checks printful_catalog_id. If that is set, it returns { syncProductId: 0, catalogProductId: printful_catalog_id } — no Printful API call, no sync product lookup. The mockup route uses catalogProductId to call /mockup-generator/create-task/{catalogProductId}, which is exactly what the batch pipeline already does.

5. Legacy printful_sync regression result
All legacy sync products with printful_id set continue to resolve via the existing path. The new catalog_builder branch is only entered when printful_id is null. 37/37 regression tests pass including explicit legacy sync coverage.

## Prompt:
should product selection be multi selection when building a catalog?

## Response:
gpt-5-6

Yes — **for CountyBuys, I think product selection should support multi-select**, but it should be a separate **catalog-building mode**, not replace the existing single-product workflow.

The distinction matters:

```text
SINGLE PRODUCT MODE
1 Product → variants → design → production → pricing → review

MULTI-PRODUCT MODE
Multiple Products
       ↓
Shared Design
       ↓
Product-specific variants/costs
       ↓
Product-specific production validation
       ↓
Review Matrix
       ↓
Create multiple draft products
```

For example, suppose you have the **Still Original Grandpa** design. You shouldn't have to repeat the entire Catalog Builder four times just to put it on:

```text
☑ Everyday Graphic Tee        From $11.92
☑ Premium Long Sleeve         From $23.72
☑ Hoodie                      From $XX.XX
☑ Sweatshirt                  From $XX.XX
☐ Dad Hat                     From $XX.XX
```

After selecting products, the builder could produce a matrix:

| Product | Technique | Selected variants | Provider cost | Retail | Artwork | Status |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Everyday Tee | DTG | 47 | $11.92–$15.92 | $29.99–$33.99 | Grandpa | ✅ |
| Long Sleeve | DTFILM | 6 | $23.72–$27.72 | $60.99–$64.99 | Grandpa | ✅ |
| Hoodie | DTG | 20 | $X–$Y | $X–$Y | Grandpa | ⚠ |
| Hat | Embroidery | 1 | $X | $X | Grandpa | ❌ incompatible |

That's actually very close to what your **Batch Generator already proved**, which is why I wouldn't invent a second batch architecture inside Catalog Builder.

### The key UX design

I'd make the beginning of `/admin/catalog-builder` offer:

**Create One Product**  
For careful individual product creation and editing.

**Build a Product Collection**  
Select several Printful products and apply a design across them.

Then Product Selection becomes multi-select only in the second mode.

That avoids a UX problem where clicking a product unexpectedly adds it to a basket when the operator merely wants to create one shirt.

### Cost should absolutely be visible here

And this strengthens your earlier idea. The multi-product selection screen should show the commercial information **before you select anything**:

```text
┌────────────────────────────┐
│ Bella + Canvas 3001        │
│ Everyday Graphic Tee       │
│                            │
│ Provider cost from $11.92  │
│ Suggested retail $29.99+   │
│ DTG • DTF                  │
│                            │
│ 628 catalog variants       │
│                            │
│ ☑ ADD TO BUILD             │
└────────────────────────────┘
```

Then you can make a business decision before entering the designer.

### But multi-select should NOT mean identical configuration

This is important.

Selecting:

```text
Tee + Long Sleeve + Hoodie + Hat
```

must **not** blindly copy the same production settings across all four.

Each product still needs its own:

- Printful catalog product ID
- available variants
- provider costs
- production technique
- placement
- print area
- artwork positioning
- DPI validation
- pricing
- ProductSpecification

So internally it should remain:

```text
                DESIGN
                   │
       ┌───────────┼───────────┐
       ↓           ↓           ↓
     Tee Spec   Hoodie Spec   Hat Spec
       │           │           │
    validate     validate     validate
       │           │           │
      PASS       WARNING       FAIL
```

The operator approves the resulting products individually or in bulk.

### This also answers a larger architecture question

You now have two interfaces that are starting to overlap:

```text
Catalog Builder
     │
     └── sophisticated single-product creation

Batch Generator
     │
     └── design × recipe mass-product creation
```

I wouldn't let them evolve into two completely separate systems.

Longer term I'd make `/admin/catalog-builder` the **human-facing product creation workspace**, while the existing Recipe/Batch/ProductSpecification infrastructure remains the engine underneath it.

So you could eventually do:

```text
/admin/catalog-builder

[ Create One Product ]

[ Create Multiple Products ]

[ Create From Recipe ]

[ Create From Batch ]
```

All four ultimately converge on:

```text
ProductSpecification
        ↓
Validation
        ↓
Dry Run
        ↓
Product Creation Engine
        ↓
Draft Product(s)
```

That's cleaner than maintaining four ways of creating products.

**So yes: add multi-product selection.** But make it an explicit **“Build Multiple Products” mode**, show Printful cost and expected retail before selection, and feed the selections into the batch/specification machinery you already built rather than creating a new product-generation pathway.

## Prompt:
after this complete what is the ejxpectation for the new feature

## Response:
gpt-5-6

After Phase 11A is complete, the expectation is that `/admin/catalog-builder` stops feeling like a technical setup wizard and starts feeling like a **real product-merchandising workspace**.

The biggest practical change is that you should be able to answer **“Is this product worth adding to CountyBuys?” before you build it.**

### What you should be able to do

When you open `/admin/catalog-builder`, the first decision should essentially be:

```text
What are you building?

┌─────────────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ CREATE ONE PRODUCT      │   │ BUILD MULTIPLE PRODUCTS │
│                         │   │                         │
│ Configure one product   │   │ Apply a design across   │
│ in detail               │   │ several products        │
└─────────────────────────┘   └─────────────────────────┘
```

If you're creating the **Still Original** collection, for example, you could choose **Build Multiple Products** and browse Printful products with useful commercial information already visible:

```text
☑ Everyday Graphic Tee
  Bella + Canvas 3001
  Cost from: $11.92
  Suggested retail: $29.99+
  DTG
  628 catalog variants

☑ Premium Long Sleeve
  Bella + Canvas 4851GD
  Cost from: $23.72
  Suggested retail: $60.99+
  DTFILM
  35 catalog variants

☐ Hoodie
  Cost from: $XX.XX
  Suggested retail: $XX.XX+

☐ Dad Hat
  Cost from: $XX.XX
  Embroidery
```

So **yes, product selection becomes multi-select when you're intentionally building multiple products.**

### Then variant selection becomes much easier

Instead of scrolling through dozens or hundreds of individual Printful variants, you should get something closer to:

| Color | XS | S | M | L | XL | 2XL | 3XL |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Black | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ |
| Navy | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ |
| White | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ |
| Soft Cream | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ | ☑ |

You can select an entire color, an entire size, all available variants, or individual combinations.

And unavailable combinations shouldn't be selectable.

### Cost becomes part of the decision

This is probably the most important improvement from your original question.

You shouldn't have to select a product, work through several steps, and only later discover what Printful charges.

Before selecting—and while selecting variants—you should see things like:

```text
47 VARIANTS SELECTED

Printful cost
$11.92 – $15.92

CountyBuys retail
$29.99 – $33.99

Product gross profit
$18.07 – $18.07

Gross merchandise margin
~53% – 60%

*before shipping, payment fees,
taxes, discounts, returns, etc.
```

Change the variants and the summary changes.

### Multi-product mode is where it becomes powerful

Suppose you select five products for one design.

The builder should eventually show you something like:

| Product | Variants | Cost | Retail | Production | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Everyday Tee | 47 | $11.92+ | $29.99+ | DTG | ✅ |
| Long Sleeve | 6 | $23.72+ | $60.99+ | DTFILM | ✅ |
| Hoodie | 24 | $XX.XX+ | $XX.XX+ | DTG | ✅ |
| Sweatshirt | 18 | $XX.XX+ | $XX.XX+ | DTG | ⚠️ |
| Hat | 2 | $XX.XX+ | $XX.XX+ | Embroidery | ❌ |

That's much closer to how **you actually think about building CountyBuys**.

You're not thinking:

> “I need Printful catalog variant 4016.”

You're thinking:

> “I have this Grandpa design. Which products should I sell it on, what will they cost me, what can I charge, and will the artwork work?”

The system handles the Printful details underneath.

### What it will NOT do yet

Phase 11A isn't supposed to make this:

> Select five products → immediately create five live products.

There's still an important review boundary.

The intended flow is:

```text
Select design
      ↓
Select 1 or multiple products
      ↓
See provider costs
      ↓
Select colors/sizes
      ↓
See proposed retail/margins
      ↓
Resolve production settings
      ↓
Automatic positioning
      ↓
Validate each combination
      ↓
PASS / WARNING / FAIL
      ↓
REVIEW
      ↓
Operator approves
      ↓
Create DRAFT products
      ↓
Mockups
      ↓
Review
      ↓
Publish
```

That's intentional. We don't want convenience to destroy the safety controls we just spent Phase 10 proving.

### And the existing single-product builder doesn't disappear

If you want to carefully build one canvas, mug, shirt, hat, personalized product, etc., choose:

**Create One Product**

You still get the detailed Product Designer and configuration process.

If you have a design and want to merchandise it across a family of products:

**Build Multiple Products**

That's the new capability.

So after 11A, `/admin/catalog-builder` should start becoming the **central command center for creating the actual CountyBuys catalog**, while the ProductSpecification/batch/production machinery you've already proven does the heavy lifting underneath.

That's why I think this feature is worth doing before AI. It immediately makes the system you've spent all this time building **much faster for you to actually use.**

## Prompt:
other than AI part, what did we miss?

## Response:
gpt-5-6

Yes. Looking across what we've built from Phase 1 through Phase 11A, **AI is not the major thing missing anymore**. The core product factory works. What remains is mostly the operational/commercial layer around it.

I see **six important areas**.

1. **Collections and merchandising management.** We have categories and product content, but CountyBuys needs a first-class collection system. You should be able to create something like `Grand Life`, assign/reorder products, set collection imagery/copy/SEO, feature products, and publish/unpublish the collection. This becomes particularly important with the 15-theme merchandising strategy we've been developing.

2. **Catalog Builder UX completion.** Phase 11A handles multi-product selection, upfront costs, variant matrices and margins. After we see that implementation, we may still need the final multi-product workflow: one design → several selected products → independent positioning/validation → review matrix → approve selected rows → create drafts → generate mockups. Much of the engine already exists; this is primarily connecting the UX cleanly to it.

3. **Product lifecycle/bulk management.** Once you have 50, 100 or 500 products, `/admin/products` needs bulk operations: draft/active/archive, collection/category assignment, pricing changes, tags, search/filter/sort, duplicate detection, and possibly bulk mockup regeneration. Right now we're still managing products mostly one at a time.

4. **Provider-cost and margin monitoring.** This is more important than AI. Printful can change costs. CountyBuys should know when a product that was profitable when created is no longer priced appropriately. Store the cost basis used for pricing, compare it with current provider cost, and surface something like `COST CHANGED`, `MARGIN BELOW TARGET`, or `REVIEW PRICE`. It should **never automatically change retail prices** without your approval.

5. **Real storefront commerce/operations completion.** We proved live Stripe → immutable snapshot → Printful draft fulfillment earlier, but there's a difference between proving the pipeline and running the business every day. We still need to make sure the customer-facing experience is finished around cart/checkout, order confirmation, customer order status, cancellation/refund communications, fulfillment/tracking updates, failed-order handling, and admin exception handling. Also, from the earlier launch audit, **Stripe Tax/business tax configuration and cancellation/failure emails were still unresolved unless you've handled those separately since then.**

6. **Operational dashboards and alerts.** Eventually the admin home should answer: What's selling? What's waiting for review? Which Printful orders failed? Which products have cost changes? Which products have low margins? Which mockups failed? Which products have unavailable variants? Which products need attention? That's what turns the application from a product builder into something you can operate every morning.

I would sequence the remaining non-AI work roughly like this:

```text
PHASE 11
Catalog Builder UX 2.0
    ↓
Multi-product catalog creation

PHASE 12
Collections + Merchandising
    ↓
Organize the actual CountyBuys catalog

PHASE 13
Bulk Catalog Operations
    ↓
Manage hundreds of products efficiently

PHASE 14
Cost / Margin Monitoring
    ↓
Protect profitability as Printful changes

PHASE 15
Commerce & Order Operations Closure
    ↓
Customer emails, tracking, exceptions,
refund/cancellation workflow, tax readiness

PHASE 16
Operations Dashboard
    ↓
One place to run CountyBuys
```

Then AI can sit **on top** of that:

```text
                         OPTIONAL AI
                             ↓
                    merchandising help
                    copy suggestions
                    design/product matching
                    collection suggestions
                             ↓
DESIGNS → CATALOG BUILDER → PRODUCTS → COLLECTIONS
                 ↓
              PRICING
                 ↓
              STORE
                 ↓
              ORDERS
                 ↓
             PRINTFUL
                 ↓
           OPERATIONS
```

There are also smaller things I'd put on the backlog rather than turn into major phases: cleaning duplicate designs using the hashes we now have, replacing the `syncProductId: 0` sentinel with a proper typed catalog/sync identity later, better artwork/version history, product duplication/templates, scheduled publication, sale pricing, inventory/availability refresh, and eventually analytics.

The big point is: **we did not miss another fundamental Printful/catalog architecture component.** We've crossed that line. What's missing now is what makes CountyBuys efficient to merchandise and operate at scale.

And I would keep **AI optional and near the end**. A good AI assistant attached to a poorly organized catalog doesn't fix the operational problems; a strong deterministic catalog and operations system remains valuable even with AI completely turned off.

That exposes the architectural UX issue.

**Multi-product mode isn't really building multiple products yet. It's a pre-screening tool that then throws you back into the entire single-product wizard.**

Worse, information you've already supplied isn't being carried forward adequately. You selected the Bears design for all seven products, but when you click **Build Adidas Dad Hat**, you're asked to **Choose Design again**.

## Prompt:
Hat variant selection:

Root cause: isMatrix = hasColors && hasSizes — hats have color="Black" and size="One Size", so both were truthy → rendered as a single-column matrix. Additionally, some products have color="" (empty string, falsy) which made hasColors=false and collapsed everything to a flat list showing v.size || v.name — all identical "One Size" labels.

Fix: VariantMatrix now uses distinctColors / distinctSizes (trimmed, filtered non-empty) and checks length > 1 for each dimension. Detects 4 shapes: matrix (color×size), color-only (hats), size-only, flat. Single-variant products auto-select and show a confirmation. Out-of-stock variants are non-selectable in all paths.

Result: Hats render as a color-button grid. Apparel renders the full matrix. Non-dimensional products render a flat list.

Persistent navigation:

Implementation: StickyWizardNav — fixed bottom bar with Back / step info / Continue. Config computed per-stage in stickyNav IIFE. Inline Back/Continue removed from variants, production, designer, details, pricing stages.

Disabled-state explanation: shown inline below the step label — e.g. "Select at least one available variant." / "Select a placement to continue." / "Set a price > $0 for all variants."

Choose Blank performance:

Bottleneck: full spinner blocked all content until /api/printful/products resolved; then N+1 per-card summary fetches fired sequentially.

Fix: 12 skeleton cards render immediately. Search box available before load. After catalog resolves, one batch request fetches all summaries (chunked at 20). Costs populate progressively per card. Images use loading="lazy". Cache marks IDs as "loading" to prevent duplicate requests.

Before: blank white screen → spinner → all cards appear at once, costs never shown in single mode.

After: skeleton grid appears immediately → cards populate → costs fill in progressively.

Failed validation recovery:

Actions added: per-row "Remove" button (removes from multiSelectedProducts + multiDryRunEntries, no DB touch). Error hint derived from error text → "Fix Production" / "Fix Variants" / "Fix Artwork" / "Fix Details". Re-run Validation button always visible.

Retry behavior: "Run Validation" re-runs all remaining entries independently.

Remove behavior: client-state only — no DB writes, no design/recipe/product deletion.

Production Settings freeze:

Root cause: loadProduction did not clear printfiles, placement, or activeTemplate before the async fetch. On technique change, old activeTemplate remained set → !placement || !activeTemplate was false → Continue stayed enabled with a stale template. On fetch error, printfiles stayed at old value → no spinner, no error, no recovery path.

Fix: loadProduction now synchronously clears printfiles=null, placement=null, activeTemplate=null before fetching. On error, sets printfiles to an empty-but-non-null object so the spinner clears and the error is shown. Rapid technique changes are safe: each change clears placement synchronously, so even if a stale fetch resolves, placement=null keeps Continue disabled.

Recovery behavior: error shown in the stage error banner with the existing Back button available. Operator can change technique/placement and retry without a browser refresh.

Existing Phase 11A features: PASS

Existing published products: UNCHANGED

Products generated: 0 | Products published: 0 | Stripe activity: NONE | Printful fulfillment orders: NONE

Tests: 1019/1019 | TypeScript: 0 errors | Build: PASS

WAITING FOR OPERATOR UX RETEST: YES

### Better fit for Catalog Builder: left-side step navigation

On desktop, I'd make the builder look more like a professional configuration workspace:

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Catalog Builder                                      Save Draft     │
├─────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                 │                                                    │
│ BUILD PRODUCT   │  Choose Blank                                      │
│                 │                                                    │
│ ✓ Creation Mode │  Search blanks...                                  │
│ ● Choose Blank  │                                                    │
│ ○ Pick Variants │  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐     │
│ ○ Choose Design │  │Product │ │Product │ │Product │ │Product │     │
│ ○ Production    │  └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘     │
│ ○ Position      │                                                    │
│ ○ Mockups       │                                                    │
│ ○ Details       │                                                    │
│ ○ Pricing       │                                                    │
│ ○ Review        │                                                    │
│                 │                                                    │
├─────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ← Back                    Step 2 of 10               Continue →      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

That gives us **two different navigation responsibilities**:

- **Left sidebar:** tells you where you are in the overall build.
- **Sticky bottom bar:** tells you what you can do next.

That's much cleaner than making the top row do both jobs.

The sidebar should also communicate state:

```text
✓ Creation Mode
✓ Choose Blank
✓ Pick Variants
● Choose Design
○ Production
○ Position Artwork
○ Generate Mockups
○ Product Details
○ Pricing
○ Review
```

If something later becomes invalid after you change an earlier setting:

```text
✓ Choose Design
! Production
○ Position Artwork
```

Now the builder itself tells you where attention is required.

### I would also shorten the labels

The screenshots show that some of the existing names consume unnecessary horizontal space. In the sidebar we can use:

```text
Creation Mode
Choose Blank
Variants
Design
Production
Position
Mockups
Details
Pricing
Review
```

The actual page heading can remain descriptive:

> **Position your artwork**

or

> **Choose a design for all products**

So we're not losing information.

### And don't make every completed stage freely clickable yet

That's important because this is a stateful builder.

For example, going backward and changing the blank may invalidate variants, production configuration, positioning and mockups.

Initially I'd allow:

**current stage + completed stages that are safe to revisit**, with the existing invalidation logic responsible for clearing dependent state. Future stages stay disabled.

Don't turn the sidebar into unrestricted random navigation until those dependencies are proven safe.

### Mobile

The left sidebar shouldn't squeeze the workspace on mobile. Collapse it into something like:

```text
Product Builder
Step 5 of 10 — Production
[ View Steps ▾ ]
```

while keeping the bottom Back/Continue controls sticky.

So yes—I would add this to the current UX stabilization work rather than accepting the horizontal navigation. It also solves the visual problem visible in your screenshots where later steps disappear beyond the right edge.

**I would remove the horizontal stepper entirely**, not keep both. The combination of **desktop left-step sidebar + sticky bottom action bar + compact mobile step dropdown** is a much better fit for what Catalog Builder has become.
